newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends lower on Iraqi oil deal clearance.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends lower on Iraqi oil deal clearance.

text.p: NYMEX crude ended lower Monday after U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali gave final clearance to the U.N. oil-for-food accord, though losses were contained as approval had been expected.

"Iraq was clearly a factor, but it was no shock that this happened," said A.G. Edwards analyst Bill O'Grady of the deal's approval. January crude settled off 32 cents at $25.30 a barrel. It was bearish temperature forecasts that seemed to weigh on prices more, however.
"Heating oil is what really took a whipping since it's going to be warmer," said O'Grady.
January heating oil settled off 2.53 cents at 72.13 cents a gallon. January gasoline settled down 0.92 cent at 68.88 cents a gallon in sympathy.
Weather Services Corp was forecasting normal to slightly above normal temperatures for the U.S. Northeast and Midwest this week.
Crude managed to end the session with the least losses despite U.N. clearance for the deal that will add almost 600,000 barrels a day of crude to the world market.

Under the oil-for-food deal, the United Nations will ease sanctions against Iraq and will allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months, on a renewable basis, in exchange for humanitarian aid.
Traders expect Iraqi oil to be readily absorbed since it is being sold when oil inventories are tight and demand for crude is seasonally high due to the need to make heating oil.
Reports that Boutros-Ghali was expected to approve the deal on Monday surfaced in the market last week.
Iraqi oil is returning to the market for the first time since 1990 when U.N. sanctions were imposed on Iraq for its invasion of Kuwait.
"Technically crude looks bullish," said Bob MacMinn, president of MPAS Inc in Toronto. MacMinn noted an ascending triangle starting at February 2 on a weekly spot continuation chart.
But, a shelf of resistance at $25.70 and below will make a breakout difficult, said MacMinn.
"There is a whole band of resistance between $25.40 and $25.70 where we have had problems breaking out," he said.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
